Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Congolese rebels seized a major military camp and a spacious gorilla park in a renewed bout of heavy fighting that sent thousands fleeing, according to the United Nations and park officials. Young gorillas play in Congo's Virunga Park, which was taken over Sunday by rebels fighting army forces. The fighting comes after a tenuous week-old U.N. brokered cease-fire between rebels and government forces fell apart Sunday. Fighting between the rebels under renegade Gen. Laurent Nkunda and Congolese army regulars in the eastern province of North Kivu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo displaced thousands of civilians, according to U.N. spokesman Michele Bonnardeaux. The rebels also seized the headquarters of Virunga National Park in eastern Congo after intense fighting with the Congolese army, according to a statement by park officials. The rebels have used Virunga Park as a base but have never seized its headquarters before. The 3,000 square mile (7,800 square kilometer) park has a gorilla facility and is home to 200 of the 700 endangered mountain gorillas in existence. "Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives," the park statement said. "They have seized the entire gigantic infrastructure [of the park headquarters] which is stategically very close to the main road heading north into Goma," said park spokeswoman Samantha Newport by phone from Goma, about 40 kilometers from the fighting. "The situation is eastern Congo is very dangerous," she said. "It's the first time they've [rebels] ever had the audacity" to take over the park.   Watch as park ranger describes the violence as it explodes behind him » . Newport said the rebels have set up roadblocks so the rangers are making their way through woods south to safety. She said the gorillas and other wildlife in the park are in danger of getting caught in the crossfire. A park ranger described the takeover. "When the rebels started approaching the park station we thought we were all going to be killed," said Park Ranger Bareke Sekibibi, 29, who spoke by cell phone from the forest earlier as he fled, according to the park statement. " We are not military combatants, we are park rangers protecting Virunga's wildlife." Although the civil war in the Congo officially ended in 2003, recent fighting in eastern Congo between government forces and rebels has caused tens of thousands to flee their homes . The conflict and humanitarian crisis in Congo have taken the lives of some 5.4 million people since 1998, and that 45,000 people continue to die there every month, according to an International Rescue Committee report in January.

“Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives,” the park statement said.

“They have seized the entire gigantic infrastructure [of the park headquarters], which is strategically very close to the main road heading north into Goma,” park spokeswoman Samantha Newport said by phone from Goma, about 40 kilometers from the fighting.

“The situation in eastern Congo is very dangerous,” she said. “It’s the first time they’ve [the rebels] ever had the audacity” to take over the park.

Newport said the rebels had set up roadblocks, forcing the rangers to make their way south through the woods to safety. She said the gorillas and other wildlife in the park were at risk of being caught in the crossfire.

A park ranger described the takeover.

“When the rebels started approaching the park station, we thought we were all going to be killed,” said Park Ranger Bareke Sekibibi, 29, who spoke by cell phone from the forest as he fled, according to the park statement. “We are not military combatants; we are park rangers protecting Virunga’s wildlife.”

Although Congo’s civil war officially ended in 2003, recent fighting in eastern Congo between government forces and rebels has forced tens of thousands of people from their homes.

(CNN) — United Nations representatives and officials from Virunga National Park said Congolese rebels captured both an important army base and the headquarters of a vast gorilla reserve during a fresh outbreak of intense fighting that forced thousands of people to run from the area.

The rebels took control of Congo’s Virunga Park on Sunday while battling government troops. The park is known for its young gorillas and is home to a significant share of the world’s remaining endangered mountain gorillas.

The clashes erupted after a fragile cease-fire, arranged by the United Nations only about a week earlier between rebel and government forces, collapsed on Sunday. Michele Bonnardeaux, a U.N. spokeswoman, said fighting in the eastern North Kivu province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo between Congolese army troops and rebels loyal to renegade Gen. Laurent Nkunda drove thousands of civilians from their homes.

Park officials said in a statement that the rebels captured Virunga National Park’s headquarters in eastern Congo after fierce combat with the Congolese army. Although the rebel fighters had previously operated from inside Virunga Park, they had never before taken over its main offices.

Virunga covers about 3,000 square miles, or 7,800 square kilometers. It includes a gorilla facility and shelters 200 of the roughly 700 endangered mountain gorillas still living in the world.

“Over 50 rangers were forced to flee into the forests and abandon the park station, in fear of their lives,” the park’s statement said.

Speaking by telephone from Goma, around 40 kilometers from the fighting, park spokeswoman Samantha Newport said the rebels had taken control of the park headquarters’ entire large complex, which she described as strategically located near the main road leading north into Goma.

“The situation in eastern Congo is very dangerous,” Newport said. She added that this was the first time the rebels had shown the “audacity” to seize the park.

Newport said the rebels had established roadblocks, forcing park rangers to move through the forest toward the south in search of safety. She also warned that the gorillas and other animals inside the park could be harmed if they were caught in the fighting.

One ranger described the moment the rebels arrived.

“When the rebels started approaching the park station we thought we were all going to be killed,” said 29-year-old Park Ranger Bareke Sekibibi, who spoke by mobile phone from the forest as he fled, according to the park statement. “We are not military combatants, we are park rangers protecting Virunga’s wildlife.”

Congo’s civil war formally ended in 2003, but renewed clashes in the country’s east between government soldiers and rebel groups have recently forced tens of thousands of people to leave their homes.

According to a January report from the International Rescue Committee, the conflict and related humanitarian emergency in Congo have killed about 5.4 million people since 1998, and an estimated 45,000 people continue to die there each month.

*Note: The following is a CNN-style news article draft based on the scenario described. Quotes are written as illustrative placeholders unless verified statements are provided.*

---

## Congolese rebels seize military camp and Virunga National Park headquarters, officials say

**GOMA, Democratic Republic of Congo** — Rebels in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have captured a military camp and overrun the headquarters of Virunga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that is home to some of the world’s last remaining endangered mountain gorillas, according to local officials and park staff.

The assault, which unfolded near the park’s central sector, forced soldiers to retreat and sent civilians fleeing from nearby communities, adding to a worsening displacement crisis in North Kivu province.

Park officials said administrative buildings at the Virunga headquarters were taken after heavy fighting in the area. It was not immediately clear whether any park employees had been injured or abducted, but several rangers were reported to have withdrawn to safer positions.

“We are deeply concerned for our staff, the surrounding communities and the wildlife under our protection,” a park official said. “Virunga has survived decades of conflict, but every attack puts lives and conservation work at grave risk.”

### Civilians flee as fighting spreads

Witnesses described families leaving their homes on foot, carrying mattresses, cooking pots and bundles of clothing as gunfire echoed from the direction of the military camp. Many headed toward already overcrowded displacement sites around Goma and other towns in North Kivu.

Humanitarian groups have warned that renewed fighting in eastern Congo has left hundreds of thousands of people without adequate shelter, food, clean water or medical care.

“We left everything behind,” said one displaced resident who fled with her children. “We do not know when we can return, or if our home will still be there.”

The capture of the military position could give the rebels control over a key route near the park, complicating both army operations and humanitarian access.

### Threat to endangered gorillas

Virunga National Park, Africa’s oldest national park, is one of the most biodiverse protected areas on the continent. It shelters endangered mountain gorillas, as well as elephants, chimpanzees, lions and rare bird species.

Conservationists said the immediate risk to gorillas may depend on where fighting moves next. Mountain gorillas are closely monitored by ranger teams, but conflict can block patrols, disrupt veterinary care and increase the threat of poaching or habitat destruction.

“Our rangers know these gorilla families by sight,” a senior ranger said. “When we cannot patrol, we cannot protect them. The animals may not understand the war, but they suffer from it.”

Virunga’s rangers have long worked under dangerous conditions. More than 200 rangers have been killed in the line of duty over the park’s history, many in attacks linked to armed groups operating in the region.

### Park operations disrupted

The seizure of the headquarters has disrupted conservation and security operations, according to park staff. Communications with some field posts were said to be intermittent, and nonessential personnel were being moved where possible.

A park spokesperson said emergency plans had been activated.

“Our priority is the safety of our employees and neighboring communities,” the spokesperson said. “We are also working to maintain contact with ranger units responsible for monitoring critical wildlife zones.”

The Congolese army has not publicly confirmed the full extent of the losses. Rebel representatives were not immediately reachable for comment.

### Long-running conflict in eastern Congo

Eastern Congo has endured decades of violence involving armed groups, local militias and foreign-backed rebel movements. North Kivu, which borders Rwanda and Uganda, has been one of the hardest-hit provinces.

The region’s insecurity has repeatedly threatened Virunga, where armed groups have used forested areas for cover and illegal activities, including charcoal trafficking, mining and poaching.

The latest rebel advance comes amid escalating clashes that have drawn international concern and renewed calls for a ceasefire.

For displaced families and park workers, the immediate concern is survival.

“We have protected this park through wars before,” one ranger said. “But we need peace to do our work. Without peace, the people, the rangers and the gorillas are all in danger.”

**BREAKING NEWS — Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo**

Renewed fighting has erupted in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo after a U.N.-brokered cease-fire between government forces and rebels loyal to Laurent Nkunda collapsed, raising fears of a wider humanitarian crisis in the volatile North Kivu province.

Witnesses and local officials report heavy clashes between the Congolese army and Nkunda’s National Congress for the Defence of the People, or CNDP, near key towns north of Goma. The fighting has sent thousands of civilians fleeing toward already overcrowded displacement camps, with aid agencies warning that access to vulnerable communities is becoming increasingly difficult.

In a major development, rebel forces have reportedly taken control of parts of **Virunga National Park**, Africa’s oldest national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park is home to endangered mountain gorillas and has long been caught in the crossfire between armed groups, government troops and local militias.

U.N. peacekeepers in the region are attempting to prevent the violence from spreading toward Goma, the provincial capital, but the collapse of the cease-fire has dealt a serious blow to international efforts to stabilize the region. The United Nations had been mediating between the Congolese government and rebel leaders in an effort to halt weeks of fighting.

Nkunda’s rebels accuse the government of failing to protect ethnic Tutsis from hostile militias, including remnants of Rwandan Hutu forces linked to the 1994 genocide. Kinshasa, in turn, accuses Nkunda of attempting to seize territory and destabilize the east with outside support.

Humanitarian organizations say the renewed combat threatens to worsen one of the world’s most persistent displacement crises. Roads have been cut off, relief convoys delayed, and civilians are reportedly trapped between shifting front lines.

The U.N. mission in Congo is calling for an immediate halt to hostilities and urging both sides to return to negotiations. But with rebel fighters advancing and government forces regrouping, the situation on the ground remains highly unstable.

counterfactuals.output:
**GOMA, Democratic Republic of Congo (CNN) —** Rebel advances in eastern Congo’s North Kivu province are deepening one of the world’s most neglected humanitarian crises while raising new fears for Virunga National Park, the fragile refuge that is home to some of the planet’s last remaining mountain gorillas.

Fighting involving the M23 rebel group and Congolese forces has pushed civilians from towns and villages across North Kivu, sending families toward already overcrowded displacement sites around Goma, the provincial capital near the Rwandan border. Aid workers say the latest movements have strained food supplies, medical care and clean water access in camps where cholera, malnutrition and sexual violence were already major concerns.

The conflict is unfolding on the edge of Virunga, Africa’s oldest national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The park forms part of the wider Virunga Massif, one of only two places on Earth where mountain gorillas survive in the wild. Conservation groups estimate there are just over 1,000 mountain gorillas left globally, with roughly 600 living in the Virunga Massif across Congo, Rwanda and Uganda.

Park staff and conservation monitors have warned that renewed insecurity can disrupt ranger patrols, veterinary interventions and anti-poaching efforts. Virunga’s rangers have long worked in one of the world’s most dangerous conservation landscapes, where armed groups, illegal charcoal production, poaching and land pressure have threatened wildlife and communities alike.

The human toll in Congo is staggering. Decades of conflict, disease and displacement linked to violence in the country have contributed to one of the deadliest crises since World War II, with humanitarian and research groups frequently citing death toll estimates in the millions — commonly more than 5 million, and in some analyses more than 6 million, since the late 1990s.

The latest rebel gains have intensified fears that more civilians could be trapped between front lines. Many displaced people have fled multiple times, carrying mattresses, cooking pots and children on foot along roads where shelling and checkpoints can make movement perilous.

The M23 rebellion, which Congo accuses Rwanda of supporting, has become one of the most serious security challenges in the region in years. Rwanda has repeatedly denied backing the rebels and accuses Congolese authorities of failing to address armed groups hostile to Kigali. Regional mediation efforts have produced ceasefire announcements, but fighting has repeatedly resumed.

For residents of North Kivu, the consequences are immediate and brutal: abandoned farms, rising food prices, closed schools and clinics, and camps expanding across volcanic terrain outside Goma. For Virunga, the danger is that insecurity could roll back years of conservation gains for an endangered species whose survival depends on constant protection.

Humanitarian agencies say more funding and secure access are urgently needed to reach displaced families. Conservationists say the same instability that threatens people also threatens the park’s wildlife — underscoring how closely eastern Congo’s humanitarian and environmental crises are linked.

**Rebels overrun Virunga Park headquarters in eastern Congo amid renewed fighting**

Rebel fighters in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo overran the headquarters of Virunga National Park, one of Africa’s most important conservation areas, as clashes intensified near the front lines of a long-running regional conflict rooted in the aftermath of Congo’s civil wars.

The rebels seized the park’s main headquarters at Rumangabo, a strategic site in North Kivu province that has repeatedly been caught between armed groups and government forces.
